2.3.3.1-r1.burton_quote: no burden (saith Menander) so intolerable as poverty

citations.display: Valerius Maximus, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*, book 1, chapter 7

2.3.3.1-r10.translation: Gyges, puffed up with the kingdom of Lydia, sent to ask Apollo whether any mortal was happier than he. Apollo preferred Aglaus of Arcadia, a very poor man, who had never gone beyond the bounds of his own field, content with his farm.

2.3.3.1-r11.burton_quote: nor infelicity to be subject to the law of nature

2.3.3.1-r12.burton_quote: And if you study Philosophy aright, saith Madaurensis, whatsoever is beyond this moderation, is not useful, but troublesome

2.3.3.1-r14.burton_quote: And surely the beggar was very merry, but I was heavy: he was secure, but I timorous. And if any man should ask me now, whether I had rather be merry, or still so solicitous and sad, I should say, merry. If he should ask me again, whether I had rather be as I am, or as this beggar was, I should sure choose to be as I am, tortured still with cares and fears; but out of peevishness and not out of truth

2.3.3.1-r15.burton_quote: No man should commend poverty, but he that is poor

2.3.3.1-r16.burton_quote: the devil had his goods, he sat on the muckhill and kept his good name; he lost his children, health, friends, but he kept his innocency; he lost his money, but he kept his confidence in God, which was better than any treasure

2.3.3.1-r17.burton_quote: and be not molested as every fool is
2.3.3.1-r17.translation: Seeing these things, practise philosophy of your own accord,

2.3.3.1-r19.burton_quote: Thou art now in the vale of misery, in poverty, in agony, in temptation; rest, eternity, happiness, immortality shall be thy reward

2.3.3.1-r2.burton_quote: the sequel of riches is pride, riot, intemperance, arrogancy, fury, and all irrational courses

2.3.3.1-r21.burton_quote: A wise man’s mind as Seneca holds, is like the state of the world above the moon, ever serene

2.3.3.1-r22.burton_quote: Everything, saith Epictetus, hath two handles, the one to be held by, the other not: ’tis in our choice to take and leave whether we will

2.3.3.1-r3.burton_quote: that they were much mistaken in supposing such happiness in riches; you see the best (said he), but you know not their several gripings and discontents

2.3.3.1-r4.burton_quote: and who can reckon half? If you but knew their fears, cares, anguish of mind and vexation, to which they are subject, you would hereafter renounce all riches

2.3.3.1-r5.burton_quote: He is exposed to hatred, envy, peril and treason, fear of death, of degradation, &c.
2.3.3.1-r5.translation: exposed to the eyes of all; always anxious; the plaything of fortune.

2.3.3.1-r6.burton_quote: they fat themselves like so many hogs, as Aeneas Silvius observes, that when they are full fed, they may be devoured

2.3.3.1-r7.burton_quote: All excess, as Epictetus argues, will cause a dislike; sweet will be sour

2.3.3.1-r8.burton_quote: sister of innocency, and an upright mind
